passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 2
passages.content:
Over the past decade, thousands of patents have been granted for what are called business methods. Amazon.com received one for its "1-Click" online payment system. Merrill Lynch got legal protection for an asset allocation strategy. One inventor patented a technique for lifting a box.

Now the nation's top patent court appears completely ready to scale back on business-method patents, which have been controversial ever since they were first authorized 10 years ago. In a move that has intellectual-property lawyers abuzz, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit said it would use a particular case to conduct a broad review of business-method patents. In re Bilski, as the case is known, is "a very big deal," says Dennis D. Crouch of the University of Missouri School of Law. It "has the potential to eliminate an entire class of patents."

Curbs on business-method claims would be a dramatic about-face, because it was the Federal Circuit itself that introduced such patents with its 1998 decision in the so-called State Street Bank case, approving a patent on a way of pooling mutual-fund assets. That ruling produced an explosion in business-method patent filings. Companies raced to add patents to their files, if only as a defensive move against rivals that might beat them to the punch. In 2005, IBM noted in a court filing that it had been issued more than 300 business-method patents, even as they took positions in other forums calling for their elimination.

The Federal Circuit issued an unusual order stating that the case would be heard by all 12 of the court's judges, rather than a typical panel of three, and that one issue it wants to evaluate is whether it should "reconsider" its State Street Bank ruling. The Federal Circuit's action comes in the wake of a series of recent decisions by the Supreme Court that has narrowed the scope of protections for patents in other areas.

The judges on the Federal Circuit are "reacting to the Supreme Court's anti-patent tone," says Harold C. Wegner, a patent attorney and professor at George Washington University Law School. But the court may also be seeking to head off a more sweeping rejection of business-method patents by the high court.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 3
passages.content:
In his book The Tipping Point, Malcolm Gladwell argues that social epidemics are driven in large part by the actions of a tiny minority of exceptional people, often called "influentials". According to Gladwell, these rare individuals possess special gifts of persuasion, charisma, or social connectivity that allow them to spark nationwide trends and transform collective behavior.

The supposed importance of influentials derives from a plausible-sounding but largely untested theory called the "two-step flow of communication": Information flows from the media to the influentials and from them to everyone else. Marketers and politicians have embraced this idea wholeheartedly, spending billions trying to find and persuade these influential opinion leaders.

In fact, they don't seem to be required at all. Building on basic truths about interpersonal influence, researchers studied the dynamics of social contagion by conducting thousands of computer simulations. They found that whether a trend takes off depends far less on the personal characteristics of the person who sparks it than on the susceptibility of the surrounding network.

A critical mass of easily influenced people is what really matters. If the network contains enough connected individuals who are ready to accept and pass along the new idea, even an ordinary person can trigger a cascade. Conversely, if the network is resistant, not even the most charismatic influencer will be able to start an epidemic.

passages.content:
Bankers have been blaming themselves for their troubles in public. Behind the scenes, however, they have pointed fingers at an external culprit: accounting rules. In particular, they attacked the standard known as "mark-to-market", which requires financial institutions to value assets at current market prices rather than historical cost, arguing that fire-sale prices in panic-stricken markets forced banks into unnecessary insolvencies.

After a bruising encounter with Congress, America's Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) agreed to soften the rules. Under the revised guidelines, banks are given greater leeway to value toxic mortgage securities using internal models rather than distressed market prices, restoring what the board calls "the use of judgment by management."

The decision brought immediate relief to financial firms, boosting reported balance sheets and allowing several large lenders to declare profitable quarters. But the capitulation has alarmed accounting purists, who warn that softening fair-value standards creates an illusion of health and obscures the true extent of banking sector losses.

European politicians and lenders were quick to demand identical concessions from their own regulatory bodies. By politicizing accounting standards, governments risk undermining investor confidence in corporate reports at the very moment when transparency is most urgently needed to restore market stability.
